idea-plugin.description:
Tasklane keeps a to-do list inside your project, one per repository, next to the code it talks about. No account, no server, no network call: tasks live in a local database under .idea/tasklane/, which the plugin keeps out of version control for you, while the workflow you configure — states and priorities — can be committed and shared with your team.

It is built for the notes you take while you code — the ones that never survive the trip to an external tracker — and it stays fast with a million of them.

The tool window

  • States are tabs in a row above the search field, each with a live count (ToDo 5). The count comes from the same pass that fills the list, so it always agrees with the search and the view filter. Every tab keeps its own selection and folded groups, and the tab you left open comes back when you reopen the project.
  • A toolbar with New Task — a split button: the body creates in the current tab, the arrow lets you pick another target state —, Edit, Delete, Group By, Search All Repositories, Open Board, Export and Settings.
  • A repository selector and a view filter in the window header. The filter shows All tasks, Open, Overdue or Bookmarked, stacks with the search instead of replacing it, and is remembered.
  • Group by date, priority or tag — or not at all — chosen per state. By date: Today, then one section per day that has tasks, each with its date (Sep 14, Sep 10, 2025), and No date last, against the date the state anchors on: created, updated or completed. By priority: highest first, only priorities with tasks. By tag: a task with two tags appears under both, untagged tasks in a group at the end.
  • Every header folds with a click on its chevron or with ←/→, and shows how many tasks it holds. Today is shown even when empty — No tasks today · You're all caught up! — because that is exactly what you came to check.
  • Archive what is done: hide tasks completed more than N days ago, if you want to. Only in the list of a done state — search still finds them — and never silently: the list says how many are hidden, with a link to show them.
  • Manual order, per state: Group By ▸ Manual Order, then drag a card by the grip that appears on its right, below the bookmark and menu, or press ⌘⇧↑/↓. The list does not jump when you switch: it starts from the order you were seeing.
  • Checklists: - [ ] item lines are drawn as checkboxes on the card — in the title too — and a click ticks them, writing the x into the body. A ☑ 2/5 badge counts them.
  • Ungrouped order: bookmarked tasks first, then by priority, then the most recent.
  • Built for huge lists. The list loads a page at a time and says how many are left (4,213 more) — scrolling to it loads the next page —, groups with more than 500 tasks start folded, and all the heavy work runs off the UI thread. With 100,000 tasks a project opens its list in about 9 ms.

The board

  • Every state side by side, in an editor tab: Open Board in the tool window toolbar or in Tools. The editor has the width the tool window lacks, so this is where you plan; the tool window stays for everyday work.
  • The same cards, with the same menu, shortcuts and ⌘Z. Each column keeps its grouping and order, and its header has a + to create right there.
  • Drag a card to another column by its grip to change its state — a whole selection, if the card is part of one. In a manually ordered column it lands between the two cards you drop it on. Move To and ⇧⌥←/→ work too, and the selection follows the cards to their new column.
  • One search, filter and repository for the whole board — the same ones as the tool window.

The card

  • A card per task: a priority stripe down its left edge, a checkbox that completes it, the title over up to three lines, one line of the body, and a row of badges — priority, code anchors, due date, tags, a link and image counter, and the date. Searching across repositories adds the repository name.
  • Markdown in place: bold, italics, code and strikethrough show their style, not their marks. Underscores are left alone, because a_name_like_this is an identifier far more often than it is italics. Completed tasks are struck through.
  • Links open with a single click, in the title or anywhere in the body — even in its greyed-out lines. Plain URLs, www. addresses and Markdown links are recognised, shown shortened (youtrack.jetbrains.com/…/ABC-123) and opened in full, with the full URL in the tooltip. The link counter opens a list of all of them. Only http and https are clickable, links inside code spans are examples rather than destinations, and trailing punctuation is not part of a link.
  • Change the priority from the card: click the priority badge for the list of priorities with their colours.
  • Filter by a tag from the card: click #api to add it to the search, click it again to drop it. Tags with a colour show in it.
  • Jump to the code from the Auth.kt:42 badge, with the full path and the code that is there today in its tooltip. On a narrow card the priority and anchor badges shrink to their icon instead of disappearing — guaranteed down to the narrowest the window can be — and the icon still works.
  • Expand a card with the chevron on its right to read the whole task without leaving the list: the full title, every line of the body and the images, each one after the line that names it, and the code of any anchored block. Click an image to see it full size. The chevron only appears when the card is hiding something.
  • Select card text with the mouse and copy it with ⌘C / Ctrl+C; Escape clears the selection.
  • Bookmark a task from the icon on its row to pin it to the top of its group, whatever its priority. The bookmark stays visible on bookmarked tasks; the ⋮ menu appears on hover.
  • Double-click or Enter opens the task.

Working with tasks

  • A context menu with New Task, Edit, Toggle Completed, Bookmark, Move To ▸, Priority ▸, Due ▸, Tags ▸, Export and Delete — the same one as the row's ⋮ menu.
  • Move tasks between states with Move To ▸, or one tab at a time with ⇧⌥←/→, without opening a dialog. ⌥←/→ just switches the tab you are looking at.
  • Set the due date or the tags without a dialog: Due ▸ has the dialog's presets, Pick Date… and Clear; Tags ▸ Add… adds tags to every selected task, keeping the ones they have, and Remove ▸ takes one of the selection's tags off them all.
  • Everything works on a multiple selection: complete, bookmark, move, change priority, due date or tags, delete. Many tasks at once are one operation and one repaint; above ten it runs in the background with a progress bar, and cancelling undoes it.
  • Deleting can be undone: a 3 tasks deleted — Undo notification, or ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z in the list, brings the last deletion back exactly as it was — same dates, same place, same images.
  • The checkbox — or Toggle Completed — moves a task to the done state and back to the default one. Entering a done state stamps the completion date, which is what grouping Done by date uses.

The task dialog

  • One dialog to create and edit, so a task jotted down in a hurry is not born different from one written calmly.
  • Write in Markdown with a formatting toolbar: bold, italics, code, link, image, bulleted list, numbered list and checklist.
  • Images you can paste, drop or pick: a screenshot from the clipboard, an image file copied or dragged in, or one chosen from disk. It lands under the line your caret was on and shows right there as a preview; the text only shows [image]. ⌘Z undoes it like any other edit, clicking the preview opens it full size, and deleting [image] removes it. A missing image shows a marker instead of disappearing.
  • State and priority as dropdowns, seeded from the tab you were on.
  • A due date from presets — today, tomorrow, end of week, next week — or from a calendar. It falls due at the end of the day, so a task set for today is not born overdue; once past, the card shows it in red and the Overdue filter finds it. A reminder tells you what in the active repository is overdue or due today, once per task per day.
  • Counts in the status bar: ToDo 3 · Doing 1 · 2 overdue for the active repository, with what is overdue in red. You choose which states it counts and whether it counts overdue tasks; click a count to open that tab, or the overdue tasks. Hide it from the status bar's own menu.
  • Tags as chips, typed separated by comma or space, removed with their cross or with Backspace. In the search field they are #api. The field suggests the repository's tags as you type, with how many tasks each has, so #api and #apis do not grow side by side.
  • Code anchors as chips, each one removable. They are captured from the editor, never typed.
  • Priority triggers: typing !!! Fix the login creates Fix the login at High. The prefix moves the priority dropdown as you type and is never saved. The longest match wins, a trailing space is required, deleting the prefix gives the old priority back, and picking one by hand beats it. Only when creating.
  • Escape closes the dialog even with the caret inside the body.

For AI agents (MCP)

  • Your tasks become tools of the IDE's MCP server. With Settings ▸ Tools ▸ MCP Server enabled, Claude Code, Junie, AI Assistant or any MCP client can list tasks, read one with its code anchors at the line where the code is now and the files of its screenshots, create tasks for the work it leaves pending instead of writing // TODO — with screenshots or diagrams attached —, tick checklist items as it goes and complete the task when it is done.
  • No delete tool, on purpose: deleting stays with you and its Undo. Nothing is loaded unless the MCP Server plugin is enabled, and Tasklane opens no port of its own.
  • Hand Off to Agent in the card menu opens a tab of the IDE's terminal in the task's repository, with your agent working on that task — claude out of the box — and moves it to Doing. The command and the prompt are yours in Settings ▸ Tools ▸ Tasklane ▸ AI agent (codex {prompt}, gemini -i {prompt}…), and the request is quoted for your shell, so a task title never runs as a command. Copy Agent Prompt copies the same request for an agent's chat, and Copy Agent Instructions a paragraph for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. The Terminal plugin is optional.

Search

  • It reads the whole body, not just the title, and ignores case and accents in both directions: autenticacion finds autenticación. Results are ranked by relevance, with matches in the title weighing more, and the list shows the 200 best.
  • Operators: state:doing, p:high, repo:backend, is:open / is:done / is:overdue / is:bookmarked, has:due, has:checklist, has:tag, has:link, has:image, has:code, has:broken-anchor, file:AuthService (part of an anchored path) and #tag. Values are prefixes, quoted when they have spaces (state:"In Review"); several values of one operator mean or, different operators add up, and free text asks for every term. A half-typed operator is ignored instead of emptying the list.
  • Dates: due:, closed:, created: and updated: with today, week, month, a day (>2026-09-01) or a distance from today (<7d). A leading - excludes: -#wip, -is:done.
  • Autocompletion: the field suggests states, priorities, tags and every operator's values as you type; Ctrl+Space lists the operators.
  • ⌘K / Ctrl+K focuses the field from the list, Enter keeps the query in the field's history and returns to the list, and Escape clears it.
  • Search All Repositories — shown when the window has more than one — searches every repository and labels each row with its own.
  • Search Everywhere (⇧⇧) finds tasks too, with the same syntax, in its own Tasklane tab. Enter opens the tool window on the task.

In the editor

  • Tasks that point at the code. New Tasklane Task from Here, in the editor's context menu and the Tools menu, opens the dialog with the file, the line and the exact character already attached; a selection within a line comes in as the body. With a file selected in the Project view instead, the task points at the file.
  • Anchor a block, not just a line. Select several lines and the task is anchored from the first to the last: its badge reads Login.kt:42-58, the editor tints the whole block in the task's priority colour, and the expanded card shows its code as it is today. Type src/Login.kt:42-58 in the dialog, or paste a GitHub #L42-L58 link, to the same effect.
  • Anchors that survive edits. The line is stored with its text, not just its number, and found again by that text: an extra import, a re-indent or a moved function break nothing. If the line is gone the file still opens where it was, and if the file is gone you are told.
  • Anchors that survive renames. Rename or move a file — or its whole folder — in the IDE, by hand or with a refactoring, and the anchors follow it. A file that disappears any other way shows its badge struck through with a warning icon, and has:broken-anchor finds every task left pointing nowhere.
  • The code points back. A line with an open task is marked in the colour of the task's priority. Hover the mark to see the title, state, priority, due date and tags; click it to open the tool window with that task selected, switching repository if needed.
  • Two kinds of mark, and you pick: a gutter icon, which never moves your code; or an inline chip on the exact character, carrying the task's state in capitals (TODO, DOING) and showing the task's screenshots in its tooltip. Or no mark at all.
  • Only open tasks are marked, and a mark goes the moment its task is done. Several tasks on one line share a mark coloured by the highest priority, and the tooltip lists them. Marks work in any file, .txt included.

Repositories

  • One task list per repository. Git repositories registered in the project — submodules included — each keep their own tasks, and a repository added while the IDE is open shows up without a restart. Without Git, the project root works as a single repository. With only one, the selector hides and its name goes to the window title.
  • Nothing is ever hidden. A repository deeper than the detection depth that already has tasks appears under Other, and one whose folder is gone stays in the list as (missing) with its tasks. Moving the whole project breaks nothing.
  • Everything that deletes acts on the active repository only.

Export and clean up

  • Copy to the clipboard as Markdown or plain text: this whole tab, the date group the selection is in, or just the selected rows. With a search active you copy the search result. A date group comes out as the log of its day — ## 2026-09-11 and a numbered list — ready for a journal or a weekly report. Past 10,000 tasks you are offered a file instead.
  • Save a whole repository to a file from Export ▸ Save Repository As: CSV — one row per task with title, description, state, priority, tags, due date, bookmark, code anchors, links, dates and id, readable by Excel with accents intact —, Markdown or plain text, state by state.
  • Delete all the tasks of a repository with Delete All Tasks in …, after a confirmation that says how many. The repository stays, empty.
  • Export the repository to XML, the tasks.xml interchange format any version of the plugin can read. Characters XML cannot hold — pasted terminal output — are replaced and counted instead of failing the export.
  • Export and Remove a repository whose folder is gone: every task is exported and counted before anything is deleted.
  • Exports run in the background, can be cancelled, capture the list as it was when you clicked even if you keep editing, and write files in full or not at all.

Images

  • Stored at their original size, next to the tasks of their repository: a pasted screenshot as a lossless PNG, a dropped or copied file byte for byte. Each file is named after the SHA-256 of its content, so the same image in two tasks is stored once.
  • The list paints thumbnails and never decodes a large original; the full image opens on click, loaded in the background.
  • Unused images are cleaned up on their own, a day after the last task stopped pointing at them.
  • Settings shows how much the active repository's images weigh, with Delete Unused Images to clean up right away and Delete All Images… to empty them after a confirmation (tasks are left untouched).
  • A warning when a repository's images pass a threshold — 5 GB by default, configurable or off. It never deletes anything.

Settings → Tools → Tasklane

  • States, as a table: name, default state for new tasks, whether it means done, how it groups its tasks and which date it groups by. The order is the order of the tabs: drag a row by its handle or use the arrows. Deleting a state asks where its tasks should go, and making a state terminal offers to fill in completion dates from the last modification. Three more checkboxes per state are yours alone, not shared with the project: whether it has a tab in the tool window, a column on the board, and a count in the status bar. Out of the box every state shows in the tool window and on the board.
  • Priorities, highest first as in the tool window: name, default, trigger, and a colour for light and dark themes picked with the platform colour picker. Drag rows to change the priority order; deleting one asks where its tasks should go.
  • Tags of the active repository, most used first, with how many tasks each has: rename one in its cell — to an existing name to merge the two —, delete it from its tasks or give them another tag instead, and give it an optional colour for light and dark themes. Renaming does not touch the tasks' modification date.
  • Nothing is written until Apply — Cancel leaves the project as it was —, and mistakes are flagged first: blank names, two priorities with the same trigger, a trigger with a space. There is always at least one state and one priority.
  • Priority triggers can be turned off altogether.
  • Repository depth: how deep to look for repositories under the project root — a view filter, never a delete.
  • Code anchor marks: gutter icon, inline chip or none. This one is yours alone and is not shared with the project.
  • Due dates: turn the overdue / due-today reminder on or off. Yours alone, like the anchor marks.
  • Status bar: whether the widget counts overdue tasks — which states it counts is a column of the states table. Yours alone too.
  • Completed tasks: hide tasks completed more than N days ago from the list of a done state, or show them all (the default). Yours alone.
  • Images: their weight for the active repository, the two clean-up buttons and the warning threshold.
  • AI agent: the command and the prompt of Hand Off to Agent, whether the task moves to in progress, and the button that copies the instructions for CLAUDE.md. Yours alone, for every project.
  • Save as template for new projects, so configuring per project does not mean configuring every project, and a direct link to the Keymap.

From anywhere in the IDE

  • Quick Add with ⌘⌥R / Ctrl+Alt+R opens the full task dialog without going through the tool window; the task lands in the active repository. It is also in the Tools menu.
  • Every action is in Search Everywhere and in Settings → Keymap under Plugins → Tasklane, so anything you use daily can get its own key.
  • Fully usable from the keyboard: Tab walks the state row (Space or Enter opens a tab), the search field and the list; Delete removes the selected tasks and ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z brings them back; ⌘⇧↑/↓ moves a task in a manually ordered state. The list, the search field and the dialog fields have names for screen readers.
  • Search Everywhere (⇧⇧) finds tasks without opening the tool window.

Where your tasks live, and how they are kept safe

  • Tasks live in .idea/tasklane/tasklane.db, a local SQLite database the plugin keeps out of your diffs with its own .gitignore. States and priorities live in .idea/tasklane.xml, which is meant to be committed: that is how a team shares a workflow.
  • A daily backup, tasklane.db.backup, made in the background only when something changed.
  • A check after an unclean shutdown: if the database is damaged, nothing more is written into it and reopening the project repairs it.
  • A damaged database repairs itself: the damaged file is set aside and never deleted, everything that can still be read is rescued, and only what cannot comes from the daily backup. Most damage is to an index, and then nothing is lost; a notice always says which case it was.
  • Tested by killing the process in the middle of an edit, the migration, the image cleanup, the backup and the repair itself: what was committed survives, what was halfway leaves nothing behind, and the next start finishes the job.
  • Changing the configuration never loses tasks: tasks whose state or priority disappears move to the default one, you are told how many with a Show them link, and they go back on their own if it reappears.
  • Projects from before 2.0 move their tasks.xml into the database automatically, in the background, resuming if the IDE closes halfway. The original is kept as tasks.xml.migrated. A file written by a newer version of the plugin opens read-only instead of being downgraded.
  • Tasklane: Diagnostics reports how many tasks and images there are, what they take up on disk, the state of the backup and the recent latencies, ready to copy into a bug report.

Requires IntelliJ IDEA 2026.1.5 or newer, or any IDE built on the IntelliJ Platform. Git is optional.
